strengths: Sound conceptual motivation: Grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis, the paper addresses a critical failure mode of locate-then-edit methods—collateral damage and poor specificity—by decomposing activations into entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic key subspaces and constraining residual vectors to salient prediction directions.

Substantial empirical improvements: SUIT achieves remarkable gains in specificity (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B on COUNTERFACT over AlphaEdit) while maintaining high edit efficacy and generalization across three distinct LM families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B).

Thorough empirical diagnostics: The paper provides compelling mechanistic validations, including component variance analysis across 5,000 subjects (Table 2), quantification of updates projecting into entity-agnostic subspaces (Table 3), logit steering via decomposed directions (Table 4, Figure 4/7), and last-token perturbation norm measurements (Figure 3).

Extensive evaluation settings: The experiments rigorously evaluate sequential editing degradation up to 5,000 edits (Figure 1, Table 10), general capability benchmarks (MMLU and GLUE subsets), and contextual robustness on CHED.
weaknesses: Ad-hoc mechanics in the residual vector formulation: The swap mechanism for residual stream projections along basis vectors w1 and w2 (setting the projection on w1 to that of w2 and vice versa) is somewhat heuristic and relies on the assumption of exact orthogonality (w1^T w2 = 0), which is only softly enforced via a penalty term. As the authors acknowledge in Section 6.2.2 and Figure 7, w1 and w2 are not fully disentangled.

Handling of multi-token objects: The mathematical formulation in Section 4.3 focuses on single-token probabilities (log p(o* | ...)). While Appendix E describes token-level accuracy for zsRE, the main paper lacks details on how the optimization of w1 and w2 is executed when target objects span multiple tokens.

Heavy reliance on AlphaEdit framework: SUIT directly incorporates the null-space projection matrix P and prior keys matrix Kp from AlphaEdit in Eq. (1). The paper would benefit from explicitly isolating how much of the performance benefit derives from SUIT's subspace modification alone versus its combination with AlphaEdit's projection mechanism (e.g., applying SUIT on top of standard MEMIT without P).

Missing computational runtime and efficiency analysis: The method introduces an offline profiling step (SVD over 10,000 key vectors) and optimizes two unit vectors with an orthogonality penalty per edit. Wall-clock editing time and memory overhead compared to MEMIT and AlphaEdit are not reported.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper leverages the Linear Representation Hypothesis to argue that both key vectors and residual updates contain task-irrelevant/entity-agnostic features, motivating subspace projections to reduce unintended model perturbation.

Strong empirical results on specificity: The proposed method (SUIT) delivers substantial gains in specificity on CounterFact (e.g., improving from 31.0% to 74.2% on LLaMA-3-8B over AlphaEdit) while maintaining high edit efficacy and general benchmark performance (GLUE, MMLU).

Comprehensive empirical analyses: The authors provide detailed diagnostic experiments, including token-level perturbation comparisons (heatmaps and layer-wise L2 norms), variance validation of the decomposed key subspaces, steering analyses for the 2D residual directions, and component ablations.

Broad evaluation setup: Experiments cover three distinct model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, and Qwen2.5-7B), test both CounterFact and zsRE benchmarks, and assess sequential editing scalability up to 5,000 edits.
weaknesses: Imperfect disentanglement in the 2D residual formulation: The mathematical formulation assumes $w_1$ solely boosts the new object while $w_2$ suppresses the old object, but the authors' own analysis (Figures 4 and 7) demonstrates that $w_1$ and $w_2$ are not cleanly disentangled and each affects both logits.

Generalization vs. specificity trade-off: While specificity improves dramatically, there is a consistent slight degradation in generalization accuracy on several benchmarks (e.g., Qwen2.5 on CounterFact drops from 91.6% to 86.8%, and on zsRE drops from 86.3% to 76.9% compared to AlphaEdit).

Sensitivity and overhead of the entity-agnostic subspace construction: Deriving $K_s^\perp$ requires sampling 10,000 entities from Wikidata (PARAREL) and running SVD. The paper does not explore how sensitive this subspace is to domain shift (e.g., specialized medical, legal, or multilingual entities).

Heavy reliance on AlphaEdit framework: The mathematical framework and closed-form weight update build directly on AlphaEdit's null-space projection formula (Eq. 1), making SUIT primarily a refined key/residual vector regularizer on top of AlphaEdit rather than a standalone editing formulation.

strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive formulation: Grounding locate-then-edit methods in the Linear Representation Hypothesis to decompose both key vectors (entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic) and residual vectors (two-dimensional target/source steering subspace) is conceptually elegant and well-motivated.

Strong empirical performance: SUIT achieves remarkable improvements in specificity (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B over AlphaEdit on CounterFact) while maintaining high efficacy and general capabilities across three distinct model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B).

Thorough and insightful analysis: The paper does not merely report benchmark scores; it validates its hypotheses through representation variance analysis, residual stream norm differences, steering experiments with the learned direction vectors, and component ablations.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: The paper evaluates both generation-based and probability-based criteria, sequential editing up to 5,000 edits, context-robustness on CHED, and general capability retention across GLUE and MMLU.
weaknesses: Reliance on AlphaEdit's infrastructure: The closed-form parameter update relies directly on AlphaEdit's null-space projection formulation (Eq. 1). Clarifying how SUIT's subspace key/residual modifications behave when paired with the original MEMIT formulation (without the null-space projection P) would better isolate the orthogonality of these contributions.

Heuristic nature of the 2D residual subspace assumption: Modeling the edit as a simple magnitude swap along two basis vectors (w1, w2) is an effective inductive bias, but it simplifies complex multi-token target interactions. As noted in Section 6.2.2, w1 and w2 are not fully disentangled in practice.

Potential domain bias in precomputed entity-agnostic subspace: Constructing the entity-agnostic subspace K_s^\perp via SVD over 10,000 Wikidata entities from PARAREL may under-represent non-encyclopedic domains (e.g., specialized medical, legal, or code terminology). Discussion or evaluation of out-of-domain entity transfer would strengthen the paper.
Minor typographical errors: A few minor typos are present in the draft (e.g., 'a entity's' in Section 1, 'feaures' in the Conclusion, and 'Insctruct' in Appendix D.2).

strengths: Strong motivation and clear grounding: The paper effectively links the Linear Representation Hypothesis to locate-then-edit mechanisms, providing a clear conceptual framework for why unconstrained key and residual updates cause substantial unintended collateral perturbations.

Well-designed technical approach: Decomposing the key vector into entity-specific vs. entity-agnostic subspaces via SVD and restricting the residual vector update to a targeted two-dimensional subspace ($w_1, w_2$) is mathematically elegant, computationally lightweight, and directly addresses specificity issues.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains: Across multiple diverse LLM architectures (LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-J-6B, and LLaMA-2-13B), SUIT delivers massive improvements in specificity (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3 over AlphaEdit on CounterFact) while maintaining near-ceiling edit efficacy and preserving general capabilities across GLUE and MMLU.

Rigorous and comprehensive analysis: The paper includes extensive diagnostic evaluations, including token-level residual stream perturbations, variance decomposition of entity subspaces, logit steering validation of basis vectors, 4-way entity-context cross-pair analyses, precomputation profiling, and testing on extended benchmarks like CHED and RippleEdits.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on AlphaEdit's framework: The mathematical formulation of the weight update matrix $\Delta$ directly adopts AlphaEdit's null-space projection formulation (Eq. 1). While modifying $k$ and $\delta$ is impactful, SUIT is an enhancement on top of AlphaEdit rather than an entirely independent editing paradigm.

Simplifying assumption of a two-dimensional residual subspace: Restricting $\delta$ strictly to a 2D subspace spanned by $w_1$ and $w_2$ works well for single-fact/single-token target updates, but Section 6.2.2 and Figure 7 acknowledge that $w_1$ and $w_2$ are not completely disentangled. It remains unclear how well this 2D constraint scales to complex multi-token generations or relational edits involving multiple entities.

Domain dependence of the precomputed entity subspace: Constructing $K_{\text{subject}}$ requires running forward passes on 10,000 Wikipedia/PARAREL entities per model. The paper does not thoroughly examine whether this precomputed subspace generalizes well to highly specialized domains (e.g., biomedical entities, legal terminology, or proprietary code symbols).

Non-standard specificity evaluation on zsRE: Although the paper provides sound reasoning in Appendix E.2.1 for using the model's own pre-edit token output rather than dataset ground-truth answers for zsRE specificity, deviating from standard benchmark conventions makes direct cross-paper comparisons in Table 1 slightly non-standard.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated methodology: The paper convincingly applies the Linear Representation Hypothesis to locate-then-edit knowledge editing, providing two principled subspace constraints: isolating entity-specific components in the key vector and constraining residual updates to a two-dimensional logit-swapping subspace.

Substantial empirical improvements: SUIT achieves remarkable improvements in Specificity (e.g., +43.2 points over AlphaEdit on LLaMA-3-8B in CounterFact) and overall editing score S without sacrificing Efficacy or General Capabilities.

Comprehensive and rigorous analysis: The authors provide extensive analytical backing, including token-level perturbation norm visualizations, variance checks validating that $K_s$ captures entity-specific features, component steering analyses verifying that $\text{span}(w_1, w_2)$ carries the bulk of target logit increase, and controlled 4-way cross-pair tests.

Extensive evaluation settings: Experiments cover multiple model families (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B, and LLaMA2-13B), long sequential editing scales (up to 5,000 edits), contextual robustness (CHED), and logical ripple effects (RippleEdits).
weaknesses: Coupling with AlphaEdit framework: SUIT computes the parameter update $\Delta$ using the closed-form formula from AlphaEdit (Eq. 1). It is not fully evaluated whether the proposed key and residual subspace projections provide similar benefits when plugged directly into vanilla MEMIT (without the null-space projection matrix $P$).

Approximation gap in the 2D residual formulation: The exact magnitude swapping derived in Appendix C strictly assumes orthogonality ($w_1^\top w_2 = 0$), whereas Section 4.3 enforces this only softly via a directional penalty $\lambda (w_1^\top w_2)^2$. An explicit orthogonalization step (e.g., Gram-Schmidt or QR parameterization) would be theoretically cleaner.

One-time pre-computation overhead: Building $K_{\text{subject}}$ requires forward passes across $N=10{,}000$ entities across multiple target layers, requiring around 1.5–2 hours of A100 GPU compute. While acceptable as an offline cost, it is an additional dependency compared to standard MEMIT.

Fixed two-dimensional subspace assumption: The formulation restricts $\delta'$ strictly to two directions corresponding to $o$ and $o^*$. It remains unexplored how this behaves when objects are multi-token entities with complex token dependencies or when editing relational patterns rather than isolated entities.

strengths: Clear and theoretically grounded motivation connecting the Linear Representation Hypothesis to locate-then-edit knowledge editing, specifically recognizing that MLP key/value spaces contain mixed entity-specific and shared components.

Well-designed, principled two-part formulation: isolating entity-specific key directions via SVD-based subspace projection and constraining residual updates to a low-dimensional target/source steering subspace.
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families and scales (LLaMA-3-8B, GPT-J-6B, Qwen2.5-7B, and LLaMA2-13B) and standard benchmarks (CounterFact, zsRE, CHED, RippleEdits).
Substantial and meaningful gains in specificity (e.g., +43.2 points on LLaMA-3-8B over AlphaEdit) while maintaining high efficacy, generalization, and general model capabilities (MMLU and GLUE).

Thorough analytical sections validating core hypotheses, including token-level residual stream perturbation analysis, variance decomposition of subspaces, 4-way cross-pair context disentanglement, ablation studies, and precomputation cost profiling.
weaknesses: The method relies on AlphaEdit's closed-form null-space projection formula (Eq. 1) to apply the parameter update, meaning SUIT functions primarily as an enhanced key/residual refinement module on top of existing editing pipelines rather than an entirely independent editing framework.

The 2D subspace assumption ($w_1, w_2$) for swapping the old and new object representation assumes near-orthogonality and simple additive steering. As the authors observe in Section 6.2.2 and Figure 7, $w_1$ and $w_2$ are not completely disentangled in practice.

The approach introduces non-trivial one-time offline pre-computation overhead (extracting key vectors across 10,000 Wikidata entities across layers, taking ~1.6 hours on an A100 GPU), which adds complexity when deploying to new architectures.

Evaluation on zsRE required deviating from the standard dataset gold-reference specificity metric to an autoregressive model-consistency baseline due to low pre-edit base model exact-match rates, though the authors reasonably justify this in Appendix E.2.1.
